reading.body:
Microsoft's Vice Chair and President Brad Smith has argued publicly that datacenters require a vast supply chain, and the country building the fastest and most reliable supply chain will lead in AI.

Smith's May 2025 Senate testimony embedded this supply chain argument within a three-part competitiveness agenda covering electrical grid capacity, workforce diffusion, and export control policy. He opposed blanket GPU export restrictions on allied nations. The framing moves the AI race narrative away from chip design alone and toward the physical infrastructure and logistics that deliver chips to compute. This aligns with the thesis that grid capacity, not semiconductor design, has become the constraint on AI scaling.

Smith speaks from a position inside the largest cloud provider by capital expenditure on datacenters. His 30-year tenure at Microsoft, including 13 years as General Counsel, means he has direct visibility into the cost structure of building and operating the supply chain he describes. His argument that supply chain speed and reliability matter more than export controls on individual components is both a genuine technical observation and a policy position that favors companies with the capital to build out that supply chain themselves.

What the data does not cover is whether other technology leaders or governments agree with this framing, or what the actual bottlenecks in datacenter supply chains are. It shows the position of one influential voice, not the landscape of debate.

standing.watch: Both cases are consolidated into MDL 1:25-md-03143 before Judge Stein, and both remain in discovery. In the Times case, summary judgment briefing closed April 2, 2026, which leaves the next step in that matter unresolved on the record. The Authors Guild class action is still in discovery, with no outcome recorded. Nothing in the records shows a planned listing, a settlement or a resolved judgment. His testimony before the Senate Commerce Committee and his regular publishing on AI regulation, cybersecurity and export policy indicate continued engagement on those questions, but the records do not state what comes next.
standing.record: The site's records list Microsoft, a public company in Redmond, Washington, founded 1975, as the company where he is an executive. Two lawsuits appear in the records: The New York Times Co. v. Microsoft Corp. and OpenAI, in discovery with summary judgment briefing closed April 2, 2026, and Authors Guild v. OpenAI, Inc., a class action in discovery. Both are consolidated into MDL 1:25-md-03143, the Authors Guild matter before Judge Stein, and both carry the date 2026-09-24 in the records. The pattern running through the record is that his presence here sits at the intersection of Microsoft's AI copyright litigation and his own policy voice on AI regulation and export controls. The records do not name him personally as a party in either case.
standing.standing: Brad Smith is Vice Chair and President of Microsoft, appointed Vice Chair on September 15, 2021 while continuing as President. He leads Microsoft's legal and public policy operation and functions as the company's principal voice in Washington and other capitals on AI regulation, export controls, and the build-out of sovereign compute capacity. He oversees Microsoft's business, legal and corporate affairs organization across more than 120 countries. He served as Microsoft General Counsel from 2002 to 2015 before being named President. He testified before the US Senate Commerce Committee on AI infrastructure and export control policy on May 8, 2025, and he publishes regularly on Microsoft On the Issues on AI regulation, cybersecurity and export policy.
